Two Hundred Years of Muddling Through review – a brisk and readable account of Britain’s economic history

Iain Martin
Oct 02, 2021
Share
Two Hundred Years of Muddling Through. The surprising story of Britain’s economy from boom to bust and back again by Duncan Weldon. (Little, Brown  Book Group, £16.15).
When it comes to economic growth, nothing much happened in the West for 1,000 years after the fall of the Roman Empire, until industrialisation gathered pace in pockets of Europe and Britain suddenly started to overtake other nations in the eighteenth century. The tale of how this damp island was a pioneer in economic progress and then exported it worldwide is a remarkable one naturally

...

For Joel Mokyr, it is about culture and the idea of “useful progress”. For Douglass North, it is about institutions, notably the Glorious Revolution and the independence of the judiciary, which controlled vested interests and which was enshrined in the Act of Settlement. For Robert Allen, it is about cheap energy, especially coal.
Duncan Weldon, a journalist at the Economist, commences his enjoyable narration of the British economy at the end of the eighteenth century and rather than taking sides in these debates, presents a brisk and readable rehearsal of events as they unfolded. Remarkably, he does not mention geography or energy much and instead concentrates on more intellectual developments.

Weldon is the author of two books. His first, Two Hundred Years of Muddling Through , explores the interplay between British economic policy and politics from the Industrial Revolution to the COVID-19 pandemic. His second book, Blood and Treasure , examines the economic history of warfare from the Viking Age to the war in Ukraine, analysing how changing institutions and incentives have shaped military and economic strategies over time.
